S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with an initial account of the event and any known safety implications. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible risk requiring a warning or action to protect people or property.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with an initial account of the event and any known safety implications. They must provide a complete incident report within 10 calendar days, updating it as new information becomes available. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible risk requiring a warning or action to protect people or property. Reports and notices must not be delayed while cause is investigated.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo sustained-heat testing at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol. A model exceeding the 5% failure-rate benchmark must undergo regulator-supervised review and corrective-action planning, taking account of test uncertainty and real-world safety evidence.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo sustained-heat testing at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, including failure rates, to the relevant regulator. Manufacturers must provide the results and failure rate for each model to customers considering or owning that model, and must not withhold them from those customers. Regulators must not publish a company's individual per-model failure rates; they may publish aggregated or anonymized results. A model exceeding the 5% failure-rate benchmark must undergo regulator-supervised review and corrective-action planning, taking account of test uncertainty and real-world safety evidence. Regulators may restrict sales where necessary to address an imminent or material safety risk. Manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers of a test result indicating a material safety concern.

parameters.quote: New home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off method. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within six years of adoption, prioritizing units presenting the greatest safety risk.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off method. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within six years of adoption, prioritizing units presenting the greatest safety risk.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally accessible shut-off method. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within six years of adoption, prioritizing units presenting the greatest safety risk. If a unit cannot be safely retrofitted, the manufacturer must notify its owner and provide an alternative protective measure, subject to regulator oversight.

pushback.text: Evidence available: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.1/100,000 last year; 4 incidents went unreported to regulators. Ember 8: 3.9% failed the 55°C sustained-heat test, but its incident rate was 9.9/100,000. 81% of installed units support remote shut-off; built-in suppression costs $67/unit; run

judge_section_notes: The final rules require strict incident reporting (24h/10d/48h) and 55°C/5% thermal testing with per-model results to customers but not public. Remote shut-off retrofit is 6 years, fire suppression 36 months, and a mandatory recall at 8 incidents/100k. The main compromises are Northwind's red lines on confidentiality and retrofit, and Halcyon's red line on suppression timing.
